what_the_eye_sees: This is the first Moloch that is an animal and not a spiked band. The four sand attempts all read as 'spiked band'. Here a sculpted creature (the 'Thorny devil' mesh) lies across the crown of a plain polished band. Face-300 carries the read. It shows a flat, broad body covered all over in conical thorns of mixed sizes, four legs splayed out to the corners, a head at the left and a tail at the right. A jeweller shown this without a caption says 'spiky lizard', and most would go on to say 'thorny devil' or 'horned toad'. That is the right animal family, so the read passes. It is not yet a clean or specific read. (1) The head is a pale rounded lump pocked with dark hollows. At 300 px it looks like a small skull or a mask with eye sockets, not a lizard's head with a spiked nape knob, and the section says no eyes and no mouth. (2) In hero-300 the legs vanish under the spines, and the body's thorns stand as a dense, upright, needle-thin bristle. From that angle the ring reads as a hedgehog, porcupine or urchin sitting on a band. Only the face view makes it a lizard. (3) The tail and the right-hand legs read as a flat fishbone or feather comb of fine parallel spikes, not as a thick, thorned, tapering tail. The thorns also read as sharp needles, where the devil's are broad-based, stubby cones. With 'horned toad' this close, the ring is at risk of being confused with Phrynosoma in the same collection.
changes: Rebuild the head end of the 'Thorny devil' mesh (the leftmost 5 mm, about theta 60-80 deg ahead of the face) as a lizard head plus a false head. Close every dark hollow and socket in the current lump. Then model a small, narrow head with a blunt wedge snout pointing forward along the band (about 3.5-4 mm long, 3 mm wide at the jaw). Put one large curved horn over each eye position, about 1.2-1.5 mm tall with a 0.8 mm base, leaning back. Behind the head and clearly separate from it, at the nape, add the false head: a smooth convex dome about 3 mm across and 1.5 mm high, crowned by two stout cone thorns (about 1.0 mm). Acceptance: in face-300 and hero-300 the left end shows a pointed snout, two horns and a rounded nape knob behind them, with no dark hollow and nothing that reads as eyes, sockets or a skull.

Turn the hedgehog bristle into thorny-devil armour, and let the legs show in the hero. Reshape the body thorns from thin needles to broad-based cones (apex height at most 1.0x the base diameter, bases 0.8-1.6 mm) that lean 20-30 deg toward the tail. Arrange them in the devil's pattern: a larger paired thorn over each shoulder and each hip, about 1.4-1.8 mm tall, over a field of 0.5-0.9 mm cones with lands of 0.8 mm or more between them (the lost-wax fill). Cut the thorn count on the dorsal field by about 30%. Push each leg out 1.5-2 mm beyond the body outline and drape it down over the band's shoulder, with 4-5 short toe cones. Acceptance: in hero-300 at least three of the four legs are visible past the body edge, and the mound reads as stubby knobbed cones rather than an upright needle bristle.

Make the tail a thick, round, tapering tail with a clear head-to-tail gradient. Replace the flat comb of fine parallel spikes on the right-hand end (the tail and the rear-leg area in face-300) with a round tail. It should be about 2.5 mm thick at the root and taper to 1 mm over 8-10 mm, following the band's curve toward the palm, and carry rings of 3-4 short cones that shrink from 0.8 mm to 0.4 mm toward the tip. Separate the rear legs from the tail so the two do not merge into one fringe. Acceptance: in face-300 the right end shows one tapering thorned tail and two distinct rear legs, with no fishbone or feather read, and the ring has a visible big-at-the-head to small-at-the-tail run of thorns.
